item.title: Day Fifty-Eight: From Surf Hostels to Hailsorms and Wonky Wheels
item.description: Trading the comforts of Salinas for a freezing forest, fighting mechanical failures in the rain, and processing the emotional highs and lows of the road.
item.content:encoded:
These last few days have served to prove some theory’s I have been creating. I’ve found myself on top of the world only to be kicked back under the table. Is it possible to have only good things in your life? Or is it perhaps the things we perceive as bad that help to create the good moments? Without a comparison can something be either one way or the other? I believe that they go hand in hand and if we want to soar with the eagles we need to learn to appreciate diving with the fish.

Day 56

I woke up early to get some surfing in, it was cold and the sun was hiding but we were leaving today and I had to have one last ride. I wasn’t ready to leave and join the ‘camino’, it now seemed a distant memory. In its place I found Salinas, it’s sunshine and the beach. For now they were making me happy and there was no need to move on. Like a dream this was a tiny isolated world that contained everything I needed. A warm home with modern luxuries, the ocean, vegan junk food and best of all sunny days. The open road in comparison was cold, unknown and difficult. This was one of the first times I genuinely did not want to continue my pursuit.

The surf didn’t help to calm my mind as I found the ocean rough and the current strong. I managed a few waves before leaving the waters and heading back to the hostel. I had some work to get done on my website and I wanted to finish it off before I left. Leaving things unfinished is giving me anxiety. Surrounded by such beauty and calmness I see now that I am the source of my anxiety. When there is nothing around to blame you often have to face the hard truth.

Noon was approaching, ‘check out time’, I thought. A broken spoke on my rear wheel still needed to be replaced before I could leave. Stress came over me and rather than accept this panic and rush I decided it was worth spending an extra day to sort myself out. I called up the hostel owner and extended by one night.

Besides stepping out for an hour to have a quick lunch I spent the whole day and evening working online. I researched some questions I had been listing, updated my website and watched some online guru’s explain their business on youtube. The day flew by and before I knew it I was looking at the clock to find 2 am staring back at me. Unhappily I called it a night and left my work space to be sorted out the next morning. This was the beauty of hostel living in the winter, instead of just 1 bed I had the whole house to myself.

Day 57

The day started off good as I packed up my gear and got ready to leave. I was slow, probably too slow. When you spend so many days on the road even two days indoors feels much longer. When you extend those two days to a week one can barely even remember what it was like out there. Granted I had travelled in the last 6 days but I also hadn’t camped and that really does change the dynamic.

The day was hot, the skies blue and I knew to make an effort to enjoy it. The weather forecast was showing rain for the next 10 days. This was the most miserable forecast I have had yet. Even France showed some partly cloudy days in the 10 day forecast! It’s not the rain so much that bothers me. My gear is pretty waterproof and I don’t really get that wet anymore. Rather it’s just that everything seems to take longer in the rain, the ride seems more like a chore than something to enjoy and mildew starts to grow whatever I fail to dry properly.

Ah, mildew! I hate the stuff, I’ve lived with asthma since I was a young child and there are only really three things that give me trouble, with mildew being the worst. I recently found some inside my tent, now its growing inside my inflatable camping mat. From experience it seems much easier to replace rather than battle to salvage items infected with this survival expert.

I was unable to replace my broken spoke after all as I couldn’t get the freewheel off. So I loaded up and went in search of something that would do the trick. After stopping at a few shops and struggling to explain what I needed I eventually bought a large shifting spanner. I put off doing the repair and cycled further before another spoke popped and I decided it couldn’t be put off any longer.

While removing the freewheel I noticed the bearings were in a bad way and I opened up the hub for a service. A clean and some new grease was all I needed but I replaced the bearings anyway. Putting everything back together I started setting the wheel true before realising that my spoke tool was too big for the nipples. A little fiddling managed to get Zen to ride while rubbing the left chain stay once every revolution.

Frustrated it was a good thing I was alone, it took effort to remind myself to stay calm and take it easy. I rode on a short distance with a the wheel looking like I was just in an accident before I set up camp in a forest nearby. Just in time it turns out as it started raining once the tarp was up.

I didn’t do much that evening as it was freezing cold, I wasn’t in the best mood and after eating some dinner I thought it was time for bed. In a matter of two days I went from on top of the world to feeling like everything was just not worth it. This realisation made me smile.

Day 58

The alarm went off at it’s usual time, 7 am is just to early for me these days. Initially the point of this alarm was to have me packed up and ready to leave my camp spots before anyone else was awake. Mostly I find myself snoozing or turning the alarm off these days. I must be over confident as I no longer fear someone discovering me. The strange thing is that I tend not to sleep through the night and my sleep is broken into two periods. This means I get some reading or thinking done between 1 and 3 am before sleeping again till around 9 am.

It was really cold outside and my sleeping bag was warm so I stayed in bed longer than I would normally. I was under a tarp in my hammock which meant I had a view of outside without needing to open anything up. This is one of my favourite things about not camping in a tent. When I wake up in a tent I have no idea what is going on outside until I unzip it all and by that time I’m up and moving. Hammock camping on the other hand allows me to watch the world go by while I do some reflecting without needing to leave the warmth of my cocoon.

Camping was strange and I had some bad dreams, the few days I had spent indoors made this all new again. I was slower at everything as my routine had been broken but I managed to get breakfast cooked and to handle nature’s call. I packed up my gear and got back on the road, despite the rain the general feeling was positive.

Squeek, Squeek went the rear mudguard. Somehow it was now rubbing my wonky wheel and I couldn’t manage to stop it from slowing me down. I ripped it off, carefully. The map showed the nearest bike shop about 80 km away as the crow flies. This was probably around the 160 km if you take into account all the turns from mountain roads. No way I could make it. I was going to be on this banged up wheel for a few days at my current pace!

My headset had also come loose and as I wasn’t carrying a 34 mm spanner I was going to have to ride slowly. With the wonky rear wheel and shaky front wheel stability was non existent. The ride was mostly rural and I never went through any towns that would offer me the required tools so even a friendly neighbour wasn’t an option.

Every cloud has it’s silver lining and I got to enjoy some really beautiful ocean views. I was high up most of the day so there was almost always a view and my slow pace meant there wasn’t much else to do but to enjoy it. I kept riding until darkness was approaching and then I veered into a small forest that dipped off a cliff and set up camp. Within minutes it went from dry to hailing and I knew I was in for a cold night.

There are so many levels of emotions that I am dealing with on this trip and every time I feel I have passed through I find there was something hiding underneath. Life is such a beautiful thing that I took for granted much more than I would like to admit. My worst days and my best days all tell my story and I am so happy to have a story to tell.

item.title: Day Fifty-Five: Catching Waves and Finding Home on the Northern Coast
item.description: Battling a stubborn cold, upgrading my route with a surf hostel stay, and finding pure joy by the ocean with new pilgrim friends.
item.content:encoded:
This last week I’ve been battling a cold, strangely enough it seems worse in the mornings and evenings. I tend to forget about it during the day. It’s definitely a motivation killer when your looking for camping spots which means the warmth of a bed seems even more appealing.

Day 52

I felt like death warmed up when my alarmed buzzed early in the morning. Despite having spent the night in a really decent hostel I still managed to get a cold. It might have had something to do with the fact that the heating was on full blast while I tried to dry my clothes, which I washed in the shower to save the 6 euro fee.

Being sick it seemed like a good idea to have soup for breakfast, so I heated up some left overs and toasted some bread. Rules are made to be broken, right?!

Marks from an earlier safa found in the hostel rafters By the time I had packed up my gear and got ready to set off it was 11:30 and another late start for me. These were becoming a habit, although without any real to need hurry I figured ‘late is better than never‘. The weather was a little strange being dry one minute only for there to be a heavy downpour the next. I suited up with my rain gear and after a quick stop at the ‘playa POO‘ I recommenced my pilgrimage.

There was a noticeable wobble in Zen’s bottom bracket which was cause for concern. There had been a few cringe worthy knocks and bumps while I climbed a fence getting out of a nature reserve a few days early and I thought I might have caused some damage. Passing by a local mechanic I decided to stop and get it checked out. Not so much for the expertise but more because I didn’t have a large enough spanner to remove the crank side bearing cup.

Low and behold they spoke no English at all which gave me a fantastic opportunity to practice my Spanish. Despite having learnt some Spanish a few years earlier while spending time volunteering around the country I never really learnt any words relating to bicycles. It was an interesting attempt at conversation but we got their in the end. Embarrassingly he also noticed that I had put my front tire on the wrong way round and the tread was causing some drag. No doubt this was the last time I changed the inner tube after 4 hours of sleep and a cold night.

Being sick I wasn’t particularly motivated and this meant a slow cycle. After walking a really steep hill I stopped near the top for some peanut butter banana sandwiches and a fantastic view. To my detriment the route was full of uphills which on the day meant lots of walking and less cycling.

Peanut butter, banana and avocado sandwich. Yum! A really heavy downpour had me seek shelter and a ‘cafe solo’ were I planned my sleeping arrangements for the night. I chose another hostel hoping to fend off the cold that had decided to join me for the ride. It was a short distance away and despite the sun setting I thought I could make it before it got dark. Alas the route was mostly off road, all muddy and extremely slippery.

When I eventually made it to the hostel I had to wake the owner who let me inside for 4 euro. It was a peaceful albergue with no internet and I had time to reflect. I was alone, inline with the theme of this trip (sense the frustration).

Day 53

Being a true albergue I had to be up and out early in the morning which meant I was up at 7 am on the dot. I cooked up my regular breakfast of oats and coffee and packed up most of my gear leaving out some tools and parts for Zen.

I had been treating a minor squeek/crack in the front hub with some lube and decided it was a good time to strip it and grease it properly. Upon further investigation I had left it too long and the bearings were already damaged. My spares were not the right size which meant I had no choice but to grease everything up as best I could and carry on. No harm done as I figure I am going to need a new wheel soon anyhow.

This was a special day for me as it was my one year anniversary since quitting alcohol. A toxic relationship that I never truly understood until after I had ended it. This meant I had to spoil myself. Even though I had already had my sandwiches for lunch I stopped in a restaurant for a second lunch of ‘patatas bravas’ before heading into the next major city on the route, Gijon.

Hill top view After hanging around the beach for the sunset and still feeling slightly sick (excuses) I decided to book into a hotel. Why not really treat myself after all?! The room wasn’t fancy but it had a bath and after adding in the complimentary liquid soap and shampoo I had a bubble bath, I was grinning from ear to ear.

I gave myself a haircut with my beard trimmer and set off for dinner in a nearby vegan spot. I really love it when I am able to find vegan junk food! Check out the Puzzle Bar if you are ever in the area.

It seemed quiet out and so I headed back to the hotel. I managed to figure out how to change the TV’s sound to English and got to enjoy a movie in my home language before dozing off. It’s funny because something like this two months ago would have been a less than ideal situation that I had to endure. Whereas now this was pure heaven, I loved every second of this newfound luxury.

Day 54

Taking advantage of the 12 pm checkout I laid in bed messing around on the internet until 11:30 before packing up and getting back on the road. This was the only place for another 70 km that I could buy camping gas so I took a 30 minute detour to do just that. On arriving I found the place closed, with a sign on the door saying they should be open. Just another one of those things I guess, plus I had been thinking of trying out these DIY alcohol stoves.

A little demotivated by having to come back the same way empty handed I stopped for a coffee when I got back onto my route. The ride was fairly easy compared to earlier days, although I’m not sure if this was just because I was recovering and better able to climb the constant hills.

I bumped into a familiar peregrino while resting in one of the towns and we chatted for a while before he went in search of Mary Jane. This was now the third time we bumped into each other and he was walking which is testament to my slow cycling, or maybe his fast walking?!

A town named after a close friend (after some modifications) While using google maps to search for a suitable camping spot near the beach I stumbled upon an albergue with really, really good reviews (‘Unmissable’, ‘Best albergue on the path’) and decided it was worth a night there. Perhaps I was becoming precious with all these nights indoors. On the way I crossed paths with another peregrino, Kang, who I had not met and he told me he was staying in a surf hostel near the beach. This seemed exciting so I said I would join him if the albergue I was intending on visiting was closed.

After 4 phone calls with no answer and waiting 30 minutes I headed to the surf hostel. The weather was going to be really good the next day so I paid for two nights. Words cannot express how excited I was to spend the next day on the beach in the sun.

The local bar ‘La Luna‘ served some vegan options which was a treat and Kang and myself enjoyed a a fun night out with good music and good food.

Day 55

It felt good waking up knowing that a day of doing nothing lay ahead. We ate some breakfast and had some coffee while watching some surf films. The plan was to hit the waves and we wanted to get some inspiration. The earliest we would get access to our rented boards and wet suits was 12 pm so we had some fun on the slack-line while enjoying the sunshine.

It was smiles all round as we hit the beach before grabbing some lunch. The day was just too perfect to describe. This was the second time so far that I have felt truly at home on this trip, the first being while crossing over to Santander on the ferry. I’m not sure what this means but I’m not oblivious to the fact that both of these days were spent on the water.

Tomorrow its back on the Camino, as Kang and I part ways. My spirits are high and I feel as though I am overflowing with joy. I wish you all the same feelings.

Until next time, love and light!

item.title: Day Fifty-One: Hammocks, Fixie Conversions, and Hitting 50 Days on the Road
item.description: Riding through Santander, repairing snapped derailleurs on the fly, and realizing how much this 3,000-kilometer journey is changing me at my core.
item.content:encoded:
I can sense changes in myself, all this time on the road is altering me at my very core. I had imagined before leaving on this journey that it would be a series of unfolding answers as I slowly but surely uncovered the secrets I was searching for. Every kilometre closer I got to Lisbon would reveal another secret guiding me in the direction I should live out the rest of my life. I wouldn’t have to do anything but commit to the trip and the rest would just show up when needed. If only life were so easy.

I often wonder what I spent my days thinking about, my mind is still scattered and I don’t feel any closer to the answers I was hoping to find. The difference is that what I worry about has changed. I find myself anxious about where I will be sleeping, where my water refill will be coming from or if I’m getting enough calories so as not to lose weight. Lately since joining the Camino de Santiago acquiring my daily stamps has been added to this list. The many years I spent living in the city has made a habit of anxiety. I feel it is time to take a step back, the answers I seek don’t lie in this journey itself, rather the journey is only a means to help concentrate on finding them.

When I last checked in I was on my way out of a youth hostel and expecting to spend the night wild camping, instead I ended up spending so much time working on my blog that it got late and I opted to try my first Albergue. I imagined it would be filled with many other pilgrims who would share their knowledge of the camino and guide me further along my path. Instead I found hip hop music and the now typical western culture wannabe gangsta’s. It was a draining experience and I was eager to leave and get back to being alone or at least away from this perfect example of consumerism and modern culture. I wanted something spiritual, something wholesome, with meaning or purpose not another MTV episode.

The next day despite the rain I was happy to be on the road. It was a tough cycle with some hills that I just couldn’t manage and I had to walk some. It takes so much more energy pushing the bike up a hill, the handle bars are low which forces you to bend over slightly and the weight pulls you back down the hill at even the slightest pause. The weather is getting warmer and my winter clothes are now too bulky and hot to wear most of the time which means Zen is looking more loaded than normal. It’s that awkward in between stage and I’m not quite sure if I need to dress for cold or warm weather, instead I focus on staying dry.

I found my way to a beautifully secluded spot over looking the ocean and decided it wasn’t worth passing up on the opportunity to stay there. Excited about the prospect of trying my new hammock I found some trees and unpacked. I slept like a baby that night, it was truly the most comfortable I have been since leaving my Egyptian cotton sheets behind in London. The next morning I was joined by many day hikers and I realised the spot was not so secluded after all, but no one seemed to mind my presence as I ate breakfast and got ready to leave.

The path forward was off road, muddy, rocky and slippery. I pushed Zen until I hit tarmac. I managed to get a few kilometres further before I was abruptly stopped on an uphill and I looked back to discover that my rear derailleur had snapped! I can’t say I was surprised or even upset, I am getting used to things going wrong. They go wrong just as much as they go right and that’s becoming ok with me. I converted Zen into a fixie by removing what was left of the derailleur and shortening the chain, opting for a lower gear ratio to save me from the hills. It was a hard ride, much harder than I imagined but I eventually made it to a local bike mechanic who had the parts I needed to get Zen back up to full health.

I found somewhere for lunch and took my time eating before setting off to find a camp spot. Just as I passed a sign to another Albergue my rear wheel seized and it became apparent that a bolt had snapped on my pannier rack. I took it as a sign to stay in the Albergue, it wasn’t a sign. The hostel was empty and while the town was beautifully quaint, camping would have offered me more. Being a weekend all the shops were closed and I was lucky enough to have the right replacement bolts. I fixed up the bike once again before setting off the next morning.

Now this was more like it. It was pretty easy riding. The new parts on Zen made her ride with little resistance and the sun was out. I saw the most amazing coastal views and got to take a small ferry across the sea. It felt like I had been transported somewhere new, like a whole new journey. Santander was a fun city with a great vegan restaurant, something which I’m finding extremely rare in Spain.

The views on this leg of the journey have been something out of this world and its almost impossible not to stay in the moment and take it all in. I have had some of my best camp spots and finally met some fellow peregrino’s.

Something is changing, I’m not entirely sure what it is yet but this trip has started to evolve…

I find such happiness from reading all these I am sure others are too.

item.title: Day Forty-Four: Finding the Camino and My Soul on the Road to Santiago
item.description: Swapping inland roads for the coastal Camino de Santiago, catching up with an old friend in the Basque country, and enduring the hardest cycling yet.
item.content:encoded:
It’s impossible to express what has happened since I last shared my journey with you. These have been some of the most trying days for me and I feel I have done some tremendous growing emotionally. The solitude of the journey has begun to show cracks in my armour and the hardest cycling yet has me questioning the way forward…

The beautiful landscape and views of the Basque country come with some of the steepest hills I have faced yet and I am finding myself walking more hills than cycling. Some of the journey has taken me off road onto clay which sucks up my tires like a pebble dropped into water. My Converse boots while waterproof aren’t made for hiking and grip is becoming a problem. It often takes me an extremely long time to climb hills as I literally inch the wheels forward and stop to prevent myself slipping back down. Without my new brake pads this route may have not been possible.

After leaving McDonalds on day 35 locating a campsite proved difficult. There just wasn’t anywhere suitable to set up and no hostels or hotels where available. It was dark, it was cold and my head buzzed from all the coffee I had been drinking. My frustration increased as kilometre after kilometre no suitable camp spots showed up.

It got to be 2 am and I was starting to doze off, things were seeming pretty miserable and then my front tire went flat. “Are you f**king kidding me” I thought as I did my best to hold my tongue. I pushed Zen for awhile hoping that a camp spot was around the corner before caving and removing my tire to patch the leak. I stopped just under one of the only street lights in site and just managed to unpack my tools before disturbing a local dog who barked non stop waking all the other dogs in the area. I didn’t know who to blame but I wanted to blame someone, I managed to remind myself that no one was conspiring against me. Woo Saa!

After being unable to find the source of the puncture I thought maybe the valve had leaked and put everything back together and set off. Unfortunately I was wrong and the tire went flat about 50 metres down the road. No light in site, full of frustration and half asleep I settle for pushing the bike.

After giving up hope I eventually camped just off the road on what must have been someone’s driveway. I raised my tent but didn’t unpack anything except my sleeping bag and left very early the next morning. It proved to be a very cold nights sleep and this coupled with the short hours meant I was nothing but grumpy for most of the day. Although I did remind myself at regular intervals that everything would annoy me on the day and that I should try and accept this fact.

It rained all day but I managed to cover a good amount of kilometres. Eventually I passed a window sign that showed rooms were available and I decided to check in. A good nights sleep was needed. It wasere that I decided, with the help of some advisers, that I would change my course. Instead of heading directly to Lisbon I was going to join the Camino de Santiago and go via Santiago de Compestela. This is something that I had wanted to do for a long time since hearing about it some years ago and being only about 70 kilometres away from the route I figured why not. It also meant that my journey would be mostly coastal instead of inland which would be a little warmer.

After eating and cleaning my gear I passed out and slept till late the next morning before heading back out just in time for more rain. I didn’t manage to cycle very far before I passed by what appeared to be a very good camping spot. The poor experiences I had so far camping in Spain made this opportunity unmissable and I decided it was worth stopping rather than risking more bad luck. Camp was perfect and despite the constant rain I remained warm and dry and my confidence improved as I began to believe I would manage in Spain after all. I slept on a slope which meant I was sliding down all night but hey this was better than a driveway and at least I was hidden.

Day 38 was hard work and I faced mostly hills. It hard to express the despair that confronts you when you reach the top of a hill only to see another even longer one ahead. The difficulty was increasing and it was taking most of my mental strength to keep pushing forward. I wasn’t really sure what I was doing and after questioning myself I found strength in my new purpose to reach the Compestela.

When the road flattened out a little I crossed an adequate campsite, close to the road but well hidden, so I prepared for the night. The next day I was within reach of an old friends house which also happened to be on the Camino. We made arrangements to meet and my sole purpose of the day was to get there. Facing more trying hills I eventually made it. I was now on the Camino and also with a friend. Happiness was again inside me.

It was a really great experience to spend time in Larrabetzu with my friend. A very open minded guy it was easy talk about the more spiritual side of life and as we are both vegan we shared many similar views. I ended up spending four days there, much more than expected. These days gave me enough time to fully service my bike, pick up some supplies, full up with some great vegan food and enjoy company.

When I eventually left I was on a mission to find a credencial or pilgrims passport. This is a document you use to collect stamps from various locations along the Camino. When you reach the Compestela they then use this document to prove that you actually took the route. I was unable to find one and as it was late so I decided to check into a hostel nearby hoping to get some information. This paid off and I picked one up the same night. Being in a hostel also meant I got to meet some fellow travellers and hear about similar journeys which was a welcomed treat.

It’s now time to get back on the road and head towards the ocean, after my longest time in civilisation so far the open road seems scary again. I am now dealing with some heavy emotions as the road begins to take its toll. I go forward with all my might as I accept this challenge for what it is and I hope to use the Camino to cleanse my soul and come out the other side a better person.

item.title: Day Thirty-Five: Wiping Out on Wet Leaves and Entering Spain
item.description: Recovering from a brutal crash in France, replacing a shattered luggage rack, and stumbling upon a starry beach valley on the border.
item.content:encoded:
It came out of nowhere. There was a sudden pull to the right and I lost control, the rear wheel slid. Every attempt to correct the impeeding disaster proved unsuccessful. I was going down, Zen was going down and we both knew it. Like a cowardly captain I abandoned ship and fate took its control.

I took my time preparing to leave Bordeaux on day 30 my gear was scattered around my friends house and I didn’t want to forget anything vital behind. We had breakfast and lunch together before I set off back into the unknown. The two days I had spent in civilisation felt much longer, it was a strange thing being around people I could talk too after so long and having access to so many shops had me tempted to splurge. I held back and only bought what I needed remembering that space and weight was limited. I did get to enjoy a vegan burger, something I had been craving. I still love my junk food!

The weather was manageable, there was a light rain but that was expected. Zen was fully tuned up and riding smoother than ever. The route was mostly cycle lanes which meant easy riding. Being so caught up in the moment I didn’t get far before hitting some wet leaves and taking a dive. Bang!

Zen’s handle bar tape was shredded, and so was the left pannier bag. My waterproof bag! The crutch of my whole journey, the only thing I had full faith in. I was gutted, my head exploded with judgements. If only I could go back and undo this mistake but alas this ain’t no video game and there ain’t no load previous save. This was going to be the way forward.

A concerned resident came out to help but I assured him I was going to live and once he realised I couldn’t speak French he headed back inside. After getting up and analysing the damage I pulled out the duct and insulation tape and made quick work of the holes and torn handlebar tape. “How long would this stay water tight”, was the thought that kept ringing in my head.

The fall had done more damage that was harder to see initially which I would discover later. The first of which was my neatly tuned gears were now out of wack and my brakes were unbalanced causing the rear wheel to stay stationary when moving. Annoyed, and desperately wanting to get back on the road I did what I could to get moving. I punished myself most of the way before I eventually accepted the reality of what had happened or tried really, really hard to.

Camp was the best I have had so far with a full tarp and chair. So good in fact I decided to stay put for the whole next day. It seemed like I was at a rented campsite. I spent the day making net from some rope, cooking up foraged foods and attempting to make extra rope from plant fibre. Time flew by much more than I would have expected and it was a great day outdoors.

Back on the road for day 32 it rained constantly. The ride was flat most of the way and it is included in one of the easiest stretches I have done to date. I reflected on acceptance most of the ride until I was stopped abruptly by the rear wheel seizing. It took me a moment to realise that the pannier rack had now completely snapped in two places leaving only one of eight welds remaining. Ok, the honest truth is I heard a problem for about 25 kilometres before this and refusing to face reality I kept riding. I might have been able to do a better job salvaging the rack if I had stopped sooner but none-the-less my now dear friend duct tape got us roadworthy.

I kept riding until I hit the Atlantic, it was a long, flat and wet ride. I was kept going by the thought of seeing the beach. It was worth it as I was rewarded with the most beautiful sunset. I took a moment to truly take in what I was seeing and I think it was at this point that I finally understood, “what will be, will be”. Being extremely grateful I didn’t mind the time passing and found a place to camp just before midnight.

I was close to the ocean, but still in a forest. This meant I was hidden and got to enjoy the sounds but not the sights. I couldn’t see much anyway as it was pitch black with the clouds blocking the stars and moon.

The next day was mostly uneventful but it was dry and this is to be cherished! I enjoyed breakfast on the beach and then travelled on mostly flat terrain along a cycle path before eventually camping in another forest not far from the beach. This was proving to be an easy ride so far and I was hoping it would stay this way as I approached Spain.

Up early the morning of day 34 my goal was to get to a cycle store for a replacement pannier rack. The thought of my rack breaking on a hill at 50 km/h plagued my mind. I passed some very beautiful towns on the way stopping for lunch. You could tell these places thrived in summer and I imagine that this particular stretch of beach front makes an exceptional summer holiday destination.

My entire afternoon was spent repairing, replacing and upgrading parts on Zen. I was in a tank top just outside the store I had purchase the parts from enjoying the 23 degree weather. The sun set and once again I was left searching for a place to camp in the dark. It quickly got late after I stopped at a supermarket on the way for a top up of my groceries. I may have been stressed about this if I hadn’t now learnt to fully trust the way forward.

If there is one thing that has rung out on this journey it is that everything will always work out in the end. Que sera, sera! Take that thought and reflect on it. You will then see the true serenity that it holds.

My aimless riding got me lost in the most beautiful of places as I found an isolated valley right on the beach. The perfect camping spot. The stars were out in full force and the skies were clear. I vainly attempted to photograph the utter beauty of this moment for you, but alas iPhones just aren’t made for night photography and all I got was a black square.

Several shooting stars passed overhead as the waves crashed on the shore in front of me. To the far left I could see the occasional blink of a light house as it did its dues. It’s impossible for me to express how thankful I was to be able to participate in such magic. Despite all the chaos we as humans create, the world is still beautiful and life still carries on as it has for millenia. If you so wished you could return to the ways of your forefathers. This thought brought me peace.

I’ve now arrived in Spain for the second leg of this journey and have to run as McDonalds is kicking me out and its time to find a home for the night. Hasta luego!

item.title: Day Twenty-Eight: A Wet New Year's Eve and Surviving the Road to Bordeaux
item.description: Rethinking camp setups in wine country, foraging for chestnuts in the rain, and reaching the halfway point of the journey to Portugal.
item.content:encoded:
Rations were almost depleted and every shop I came across was closed for the holidays. This grand miscalculation would end up costing me, yet there was nothing I could do about it now. The lighter weight and easier packing came with dread and uncertainty. Its funny, the grass is always greener on the other side.

Setting out the morning of day 23 I found myself deciding I was going to camp the remaining nights until I got into Bordeaux. I was planning on meeting an old traveller friend of mine and I wanted to rack up the outdoor experience before life got too comfortable. I was starting to feel guilty about sleeping indoors, it just seemed too easy.

I headed slightly off course in order to make it into Poitiers as I needed to get some banking done and my banks branches were scarce in France. I was pleasantly surprised to find that the town had a certain ‘je ne sais quoi’ about it. Maybe it was the architecture, maybe it was the hills and the view they offered but I found something moving about being there. This was almost enough to make up for the fact that my bank branch had shut down 3 days earlier, permanently. Onward and upwards!

Many thoughts ran through my mind as the sun began to set. Should I get a hotel, should I try for a bed through Warmshowers, should I try for a camp spot. Up until this point I hadn’t had much luck with city camping. I felt uncomfortable camping close to civilisation, it seemed less wild and more vagrant. I must have seemed like a deer in the headlights as a father and his son offered me help with directions. Was I going to break my pact to camp until Bordeaux on the very same day I made it?!

I retreated to the familiar McDonalds. Here I could hide from the decision and using the free WiFi to test out some ideas I had for my website. I ended up staying until just before closing. I may have missed an opportunity as a curious shopper questioned me about my bike and my sleeping arrangements. I definitely have some trust issues to work on as I answered all questions intending not to give too much away.

Before leaving the warmth and comfort of my booth I did a quick google maps scan of the local area and found what appeared to be some thick vegetation nearby. It was going to have to do. The camping spot was less than ideal and while it was off the main roads it was still in sight of a dirt road which was used a few times while I was constructing my home. This would be a quick nights sleep, no dinner and no breakfast, I was going in and out.

The rush to leave the next morning meant I ended up battling the wind while I cooked some breakfast on the side of the road further down my route. Despite the inconvenience of the last 8 hours I had finally camped out in a populated area and my confidence was high. My dependency on hotels for WiFi and electricity was lifting. I spent the day feeling very proud and excited about the possibilities this new-found confidence would bring me.

The weather was reported to be getting worse and the forecast showed some heavy rain on the way. My tent being still damp didn’t seem up to the task of keeping me dry. I found a small little patch of land where hunting was marked forbidden and re-purposed my ground sheet into a poorly tied a-frame. The idea was to allow my tent to dry out despite this expected rain. Unfortunately the night brought the most powerful wind I had felt so far and one of my pegs came loose which meant everything got wet again. My plan had failed. I knew then that I needed to learn some better knots, more rope tension could have prevented this from happening.

I left late the next morning after spending some time trying out some different tarp configurations and knots. My oats were finished and breakfast was coffee and bananas, the quinoa was headed the same direction. It was time to go shopping.

I was entering wine country and with it came constant climbs followed by steep downhills. I couldn’t help but think why I should climb the hill when I was just gonna go down the other side and do it again. I was grumpy and frustrated and in this moment it seemed like everything was against me. As if the world, for millions of years, had conspired against me to make the terrain particularly unpleasant for this journey right now. The arrogance!

Despite this I had found that lately my patience and frustrations with the road were improving. I had come to the realisation that no matter what I planned or expected it was highly likely that things would not pan out that way. I would have to learn to adapt to all situations, to bend the outcome to my desire. A simple concept for most but it really has offered more peace to my journey. I began expecting the worst while still hoping for the best and accepting that the weather had nothing against me. It would also not do me any favours! If I opened one bag what I needed would be likely be in the other. I would have mechanical troubles and flat tires in the bad weather rather than the good. When you start to realise that the world does not have anything against you, that things are just the way they are, that is when it becomes a better place to live in.

It was getting dark, I had run out of water and there was no place in sight to camp out. I decided to trust the road, not to stress and just to keep on cycling until what I needed came about. After riding through a small village I stumbled across an old water pump. Thankfully this fully restocked my water supplies and allowed me to do a little washing up. The weather was looking dry and the forecast said it would stay that way for the night. I found an isolated spot, erected my tent along with a washing line to dry my towels and began cooking the remains of my food. I got to camp with my tent open which meant no condensation, this was a welcomed relief.

The morning of day 26 the sky was blue and I was in for a bright day. My head was bursting with ideas for new camp setups and different knot types, My goal was to try to replace my tent with only a tarp, purely to see if I could hack it. Working with the rope had also given me the urge to make my own hammock, it could double as a chair or a bed when good weather came around. Most of my ride was spent with thoughts of such things and the creative juices blocked out the moment more than I would have liked.

I stopped in a small town for lunch and purchased some fresh vegetables and fruit, the other shops were all closed expect for a small bakery. The night would bring the new year and I wanted to have some treats to celebrate. Stopping for a quick snack, a local women approached me and warned me of some very bad weather approaching. I looked up at the blue skies, felt the sun on my face and dismissed the comment with a polite thank you and goodbye. This moment played on my mind for another hour or so. Was there a mistake in her translation or did she just mean the winter weather in general?!

It turned out a storm was approaching and just before dark the weather took a nasty turn for the worst. A frantic rush for cover meant I had to pass some wild walnut trees which was a real disappointment especially due to my low rations. I made it to my elected camp spot and expecting to be stuck there for the next two days I tied up my new and improved tarp layout. I wanted to give myself some cover outside the tent to feel less confined during the storm, plus it was new years.

My new years celebrations were the calmest they have been in years. I found myself alone in the forest listening to the awesome power of nature and the odd grunt echoing in the forest as the wild pigs foraged for truffles. I fantasised that the rain was washing away 2017 and that 2018 would bring a fresh start.

The next morning after making up a fresh fruit salad I was optimistic about the day and decided to pack up and journey on instead of staying put. My tent was for the most part dry, as was my gear. Tarp take two was a success! Mostly thanks to the truckers hitch, my now second favourite knot after the rolling hitch. It’s hard to really appreciate knots until you see what some of them can do.

On the way out the forest the rain started to pick up but I still found time to collect some chestnuts. I planned on cooking these up for dinner at some point. After gathering enough to make a decent meal I headed South. The road became continuously more bumpy as it took me a little while to notice that my rear tire had gone flat. It was not fully flat indicating a slow puncture and with all the rain I opted to pump it up and see if it continued to deflate. Maybe I could do a repair at my friend’s place, hopefully under shelter.

The rain started to get really bad and I was dripping head to toe, Zen had picked up an awful squeal and my boots were full of water. Coming across a bridge I decided to camp out for an hour or so and dry up with a coffee. The bridge was creating a wind tunnel which aided drying, but I was out of food and my clothes were still mostly wet. My best solution was to get into a big town. I had to resupply and dry up. I knew that being wet could end up causing more trouble that it was worth. I couldn’t risk getting sick on this trip.

It was a desperate push to close the remaining 70 kilometres into Bordeaux. The sun was already setting and this was the latest I would be out cycling since my first long day from London to Dover. It was going to be a night cycle. I arrived around 10 pm and a clean shower followed welcomed dinner. This would be the first time I could hold real conversations in the last 20 or so days, how strange.

I’m now warm and dry, my clothes are freshly cleaned and supplies are stocked up. Bordeaux has offered me sanctuary for the last 2 days and I can hear the open road calling me. With Spain just around the corner I’m sensing good things to come. I’ve now passed the 1000 kilometres mark which puts me about half way to Lisbon and will with so much still to learn and experience I’m sure it’s going to continue to be an interesting adventure.

item.title: Day Twenty-One: Wild Boar Encounters and the Three-Week Habit
item.description: Staring down a dozen glowing eyes in the dark, snapping a chain tool, and realizing the wild road is finally starting to feel like home.
item.content:encoded:
“The night is long and full of terrors”, echoed in my head as I found myself hiding behind a tree frantically searching for anything I could climb. The roar came again, louder this time. I was too frightened to turn on my light and attract attention, I just couldn’t tell what creature I was facing…

It’s a funny thing our fear of the dark and of the unknown. It makes sense from an evolutionary perspective but we sometimes struggle to correlate this to the new world humans have created.

When I last paused a moment to share my adventures it was just approaching Christmas and the holiday spirit had me down. Thank you to everyone who got in touch and wished me well and added to the magic that is this time of year. I was especially lucky to be put up in a chateau for one night. The place was absolutely beautiful and I took advantage of the access to a hot bath and a heated swimming pool. I truly recommend Chateau de Jallanges to anyone who needs to get away from it all and rest within themselves. From reading the notes left behind it seems to also make a great honeymoon destination.

I was up early the morning of day 20, well rested and feeling as though I had a sense of inner peace. The luxuries had me feeling like royalty and I agonised over the thought of enduring the open road, in what seemed like more rain. These extreme changes in situations are troubling to deal with, yet it is this exact spectrum that opens us up to learn to appreciate the things and situations we often take for granted.

After breakfast it was time to burn rubber and I made my way further South. So far on my trip I have found it the most difficult to camp out when I am in the larger towns and cities. I haven’t quite mastered using the locals to my advantage as explained here and I also prefer the solitude of camping wild in an isolated spot, at least when this is possible. Being close to Tours, a large city, I needed to cover some ground if I intended to camp as I usually did.

The roads began to get quieter and the landscape changed from blocks of flats with peeling paint to large green trees and open fields. I could see the vast empty road in front of me and as I turned my head the triumph of civilisation behind. Just then a dog charged towards me, barking, as they often like to do when passing by houses. The bark sounded more friendly than anything and it that moment I was overcome by my emotions.

Tears formed in my eyes as I felt compassion for this animal who I imagined was wishing me well on my pursuit. I thought of all the pleasures I had enjoyed these last three days and pondered how I would make this way of life sustainable. It’s the fear of going back to what my life used to be, coupled with the longing for the luxuries it offered. Watching Netflix in the comfort of a soft bed, tasty food at the ready, meeting friends for a coffee, these things I still wanted. Unfortunately so far in my experience they had come with working long hours most of the week, being rudely awakened each morning by an electronic slave driver, and crammed commutes with grumpy faces. These things, on the other hand, I wanted to avoid like the plague. How do you have your cake and eat it?!

All in all this was a happy day and the weather cleared up as the time past. I found a camp spot in a very isolated woodland and began sketching the plants around me. I decided the only way to get better at foraging for food was to learn what I was looking at and this hobby would fit in well with the mycology I was practising.

After setting up camp and constructing a DIY bike stand from a split tree I made some much-needed adjustments to my gears and fully serviced my rear derailer. I did this by stripping it down and greasing it before putting it back together. This seemed to solve most of the problems I was having. It was distracting working on Zen and the time flew by as I toiled behind my head lamp. The total isolation of this particular camp spot caused no concern for the light pollution.

I froze as I began hearing loud growl like noises. I couldn’t identify the noise and I had no idea what I was up against. I waited it out in complete silence until I noticed the rummaging and growling was getting closer. I took a few steps towards the noise and it got worse. At this point I felt extremely vulnerable. Was this a bear? A wolf? Some other type of biting, slashing, sprinting animal?

The trees had no low hanging branches which were strong enough to support my weight, both my knifes were under 3 inches long and my food was scattered around my campsite. The time for action was now but not knowing what to do I stood frozen for a moment, half hidden behind a tree. The noises got closer. The choice was to either abandon the site along with my gear and hope for the best or attempt to frighten off whatever this was. I opted for the latter. I put my head lamp on the brightest setting and moved it frantically in the direction of the noises.

The first thing I saw was eye’s lit up everywhere, at least 12 pairs. My heart stopped. I giggled, these were only wild boar. I was aware of the damage they could cause but I also knew they would do me no harm if I let them be. I turned around and headed back to my tent startling them away as I moved. Crisis averted, it was time to lay back and count the sheep.

The trees had a golden shimmer as I peered out my tent in the morning. I did a mental fist pump as I noticed the blue skies and lack of clouds. Everything was bone dry, hallelujah! On the road I appreciated the quick reaction of my gears, the work from the night before had been a success. Passing by a truly super, super market, I resupplied and must have been overzealous because it ended up taking me about an hour to get everything back on Zen. In the end I had to eat a good lunch to make the room.

A strong wind came against me dropping my speed to under 10km/h as I rode on long flat stretches. I began feeling a small vibration when pedalling and later identified that my chain had broken free at one link, not enough to snap but enough to cause some slight issues. The outer link must have gotten bent from riding like this as I ended up snapping my chain tool trying to fix it. Great! I now needed a new chain tool and it seemed like a new chain.

I had purchased and fitted this chain myself before setting off on the journey and since then I had learned that the speed of the chain relates only to the rear sprockets and not the whole drive train. This meant my chain was about 1 mm too thin. This explained some of my shifting troubles.

Camp was next to a river facing East which offered a beautiful sunrise in the morning. The plan for the day, get to a bike shop and replace Zen’s chain. Hopefully without the chain snapping entirely or causing damage to anything else. I am happy to say this mission was a success.

So here I am, fresh chain, new tool and ready to set out on the road again. I have heard it said that it takes 3 weeks to make or break a habit. If there is any truth to that then this way of life has now become a habit and I can expect things to get a whole lot easier. I really want to start eating more from the land and finding better ways to collect water and I would appreciate any tips.

The road is long and winding, may the call of the wild comfort you. Until next time, Safaman signing out.

item.title: Day Eighteen: Mushrooms, Muddy Detours, and a Lonely Christmas on the Road
item.description: Navigating deep forest thickets, sketching wild fungi, and wrestling with the quiet loneliness of a holiday season far from home.
item.content:encoded:
The road seems quiet, only the birds chirp in the distance. For a moment the stillness brings a sense of peace and calmness, then the realisation hits that Christmas is approaching. What happened to the days of December?! Pictures of the typical hallmark family, next a fireplace, opening presents flood my mind. I am alone.

Its not that I haven’t spent many Christmas alone before or at least ‘sans famille’. There is something about this whole experience that opens you up to all the questions you’ve been hiding away from for so long. I begin to wonder whether life has any meaning if it is not shared with people you love.

Leaving my motel on day 14 the sky was grey but it was dry and that’s all that mattered. My gear freshly packed and waterproofed I felt I could conquer the world. Before setting off I decided I would buy Zen that tent I had been pondering over and cycled down to purchase a full bike cover. I also picked up a ground tarp. It took a little bit of effort and organisation to repack these rather large items into my already cumbersome load but I got it done.

Setting off I ran into some minor but annoying mechanical problems which delayed me as I did my best to resolve them before moving on. My poor Zenny was taking a beating and it was only going to get worse. It was at this point that I noticed my rear rack had come apart at the weld in two locations and it is now being held together in three different places by duct tape. Remember what I said about the only two tools you ever need on Day One?

“There are only two tools you ever need to fix any problem, WD40 (Q20) and Duct tape.” - Dad

The little delays, setbacks and late start meant I covered very little distance before seeking shelter from the fog. I found myself in a beautiful forest just as the sun was setting. Words just cannot express the way true beauty melts away your worries and fears. This was the perfect time for a little yoga before snacking on some almond paste and settling in for the night.

I honestly think I may be sleeping too much. I’m trying to be kind to my body after the punishment I’m putting it through but with the early sunsets its very easy to curl up and wake up in the middle of the night instead. I then don’t want to face the cold at 3/4am so I force myself to stay in bed till the alarm goes off. What do you think, how many hours sleep is too much?

The night was quiet apart from the hooting of owls as they surveyed their hunting grounds for breakfast. I got up on the morning of day 15 fresh and ready to go. I knew the challenge it would be to get back to the main road as I would need to backtrack through the brambles, over the river and between the dry grass I had conquered the night before. The weeds lashed onto Zen as I pushed with all my might almost as if they didn’t want us to leave. Hooking around the cogs and grabbing onto my gear it seemed like the scary forests of the old Disney moves.

When I made it to the road I found that my rear mud guard had been badly damaged and it was obstructing the spokes. A minor adjustment sorted this, hey, its only a mud guard right? Nothing mission critical and besides I was already covered in mud anyway.

I started the ride with the bold intentions of making it to Tours the same day, about 120 km away. That plan quickly changed the moment the hunger set it. I had been snacking on some cherry tomatoes and rocket, with the aim of getting some vitamins in my system but they didn’t do much for my calorie intake so I stopped at a nearby cafe for some lunch and purchased a few supplies from a local store.

I’m not sure exactly what happened after that but I found myself on a long and steep hill and somehow managed to injure my left knee. Fearing further damage and a long delay to my continued travels I kept heading South at a slow pace searching for a camp spot. I found a nice article which I hope will stop this pain in its tracks. Dinner was followed by some light stretching and then reading before bed.

Early day 16 I was up and at it, managing to pack up all my gear earlier than planned. The weather had been dry the past few days which made this task much simpler. A quick look at the forecast showed that this would change unless I could make it to Tours. Still I had braved the rains before and this forest was swarming with mushrooms so I thought I’d try my hand at mycology, the study of mushrooms.

Mushrooms are the one area where the old saying “what doesn’t kill you, makes you stronger” doesn’t really apply, but alas we have to start somewhere. I opted not to eat anything but rather to sketch out some specimens and later in the day try and identify them. Doing this I hoped to learn what characteristics are important to take note of in the future. It turns out that this is a really serious hobby and unfortunately one that can kill if you make a mistake. Challenge accepted!

The day was a hard push combined with some amazing foods. My limited choice is starting to bring out flavours in foods I never noticed before. Even something as simple as avocado on bread leaves my mouth watering. I found a public toilet on the way and had a ‘hand shower’, washed down Zen and refilled both my water bottles which aren’t seeming to last too long these days.

Camping that night was a sort of change in thinking. The forest must have been seeming with deer as I heard constant calls and barking from all directions. Even though they were distant the stomping sounded powerful and I imagined the stags fighting over dominance while onlookers cheered them on. This brought me back to a book I read when I was a child, Fire Bringer by David Clement-Davies, and I found it comforting. If you haven’t heard the different sounds that deer make before, wild camping is definitely a great yet frighting first way to do so, which I highly recommend.

With it being so obvious that these marvellous creatures where abundant in the area I began to wonder what predators may be lurking around the corner and all of sudden the thin polyester walls of my tent didn’t seem to offer any comfort. While I’m sure it wouldn’t do much against an attacking animal, nevertheless, my trusty Leatherman stayed by my side. Appropriately engraved with the words “Never Give Up, Love Dad”

The sounds continued until the morning, mixed in with various other calls and more owls hooting. For someone like me it was heaven. For that brief moment in time, I was alive in a world that had and needed nothing else. It was genuine and wholesome. Some brief mushroom sketching and I was on my way out. Or so I thought.

Somewhere along the way I got myself all turned around and I had been pushing Zen for ages through the thick mud and leaves before realising I was lost. Of all places I have stayed this seemed close to the most wild and I was lost! It wasn’t possible to just follow my compass because of the thick forage that came up on occasion and pushing/lifting a loaded Zen over obstacles was no easy task.

I did eventually make my way out, albeit, with some damage to Zen’s rear derailer. I fixed her up enough to ride and headed to Tours, opting for main roads and the quicker routes over the quieter ones. After failing to find appropriate camp grounds and needing further repairs and parts I booked into a local motel for yet another pit stop and shelter from the violent dark. I had already witnessed two fights within hours of arriving.

It’s a strange thing looking back on the ride so far. It once seemed so mysterious and frightening but now the road is becoming my new normal. I have become used to my limited conversations and hand signals, although my French is improving with the addition of a French-English phrase book. The simple meals and lack of choice bring with it a sense of comfort. Allowing the mind to ponder over more important things. And strangely enough, aside from the minor hiccup with my knee the cycling is not that hard at all.

My greatest fear now remains that which has plagued humanity since the dawn of time, the fear of the unknown and what is coming around the corner.

I hope you are enjoying following along on my pursuit but if there is anything you would like to read more about or indeed, less about, I’d love it if you left me a comment letting me know. Until the next, Merci. Au Revoir. Prends soin de toi.

item.title: Day Thirteen: When a Cycle Tour Starts Feeling Like Homelessness
item.description: Saturated gear, frozen fingers, and a breaking point under a bridge in France force me to question everything on the road to Lisbon.
item.content:encoded:
Doubt weighs heavy on my mind. Everything is wet and my waterproof jacket has failed me. Even when its not raining its damp, humid and nothing seems to want to dry. My fingers are red and I can tell they’re hating the cold. Am I cut out to continue this journey or am I beat?! Lets backtrack a few days and I’ll explain how I got to this point.

The morning of day 9 started off calm, I was well hidden and felt no need to rush before sunrise so I took my time. After cooking up some oats and raisins with a fresh cup of coffee I began the daily ritual of drying off and packing up my gear. I was starting to feel for Zen who’s been left out in the rain multiple nights now, I need that grease to stay where it is, I need to consider the welfare of my machine. Maybe I should get her a tent?

Heading out the forest with Zen all loaded up was trickier than coming in. There was a steady rain and I just wanted to make a move on and forget about the fact that most of my gear was packed away wet. I reached the road hopped on the seat and low and behold, another flat tire. Luckily I still had some coffee left in my flask.

I pushed Zen a little up the road to get shelter from a tree and removed her front wheel. This flat was my fault. There was a new puncture but it was in a very similar position to the one from yesterday. On further inspection I found that I had not removed the thorn from the tire itself, rookie error! Laughing at my mistake I began whistling and gained the attention of the local farmer who’s tree I was using for shelter. He attempted to talk to me but with my limited french we ended up speaking mostly in body language with multiple thumbs up from my side. He promptly disappeared before returning with a freshly boiled cup of tea, two cubes of sugar and a small biscuit. I was impressed with this French hospitality!

With Zen back together and my belly warmed I thanked the farmer with a polite “Merci beaucoup” and wished him well with “Au revoir” before making my way up the road. “Right”, I said to myself, “NOW, we can begin”. After riding for a couple of hours it seemed the right day to make some adjustments to Zen. I made a pit stop and moved her seat a little back, dropped the height slightly and did some further fine tuning. It felt really good riding without her 20 something kilogram load, I felt powerful if not slightly off balance.

I didn’t manage to cover much distance over the day due to the constant rain which eventually had me seeking shelter in a local pub where I enjoyed not one by two coffees. Making my way out I hoped they wouldn’t notice the massive puddle of water I had left behind me imagining them cursing the foreigners once I had gone.

The positive side of this rather wet day was that I ended up finding my best camp spot so far. It was fully secluded, the ground was padded with fallen leaves and I was a little sheltered by trees. The rain stopped so I set up my tent hoping to let it air dry a little. Packing it wet meant that even the sleeping area was not fully dry. I got a good 20 minutes of dry time before the rain kicked back in. “Ah, why do you do this to me?”

I fell asleep quikly which caused me to wake up around midnight. I played some cards and did some planning before falling back to sleep a couple of hours later. Unfortunately this disruption caused me to sleep through my alarm and I woke up around 10am the next morning. It was raining all night, the spot was secluded and I thought it might help to dry out my gear, so I decided to stay put for the day and leave the next morning.

Most of day 10 was spent inside my tent hiding from the rain and I only headed out when nature called. Mostly I wrote in my notebook and thought about life while trying to stay warm and dry.

On day 11 I was up bright and early at 4am, I had some beans in tomato sauce for breakfast and my staple morning coffee before setting off. Nothing had dried and for the most part my gear was still wet. I think the ground sheet of my tent is failing and letting water through, it may be time for a tarp?! I’m sensing a lot of frustration inside myself and I am losing patience over the smallest things. Being wet is making it hard to sleep and I keep waking up from the cold. To top it off I am on my reserve tank of gas and out of food and water. Time to refuel!

I headed to the nearest camping shop where I could buy some extra stove gas and some warmer sleeping clothes. The whole day was about getting there but passing by a Mc Donalds tempted me and I went off route for the free wifi and a coffee. I didn’t know it at the time but this would cost me later.

By the time I made it to the camping shop it was already getting dark and I had no plans of where to sleep. The weather was, well, raining and so far on my journey I hadn’t attempted to search in the darkness for a camping spot. I made my purchases and decided the best way forward would be to continue towards Lisbon and stop when I saw someplace suitable to rest.

Nowhere was suitable! The ground was either extremely lumpy or covered in sharp, spiky weeds. All the land was sloped and there were no flat sections of forest. On top of that any ‘hidden’ spots would be visible as soon as the light hit. I carried on for a further 2 hours before I started to worry that I might run out of battery on my torches. I would have to settle. I found the least slopped section with reasonable coverage and camped there.

It was a nightmare, it rained all night. My tent was so wet it was raining inside and I kept sliding down the the bottom of the tent. I hadn’t eaten dinner and I told myself I just needed a short nap and I would set off first thing in the morning. Despite being so wet my new sleeping gear did keep me reasonably warm compared to other dry nights, you do try and find solace in the small things!

The morning came with a “Beep Beep Beep” and I struggle to get out of my sleeping bag to shut off the noise. It was pitch black outside and not raining! The stars were beautiful through the tree tops and I took a moment to appreciate nature, her stunning beauty which seemed to rival her ferocious inclinations. There was no breakfast and I hurried to get out of my least suitable camp spot so far before light came and revealed my location.

So far it had been dry and the weather report showed a sunny day. I was excited for the change and thought I would stop off at a local park and dry off my gear around lunch. Almost as I had this thought a great frost wind swept over me and froze everything solid, even Zen’s gears wouldn’t work for a moment. I rushed to close up all my zips and tighten my elastics to keep the warmth in my clothes. There was no feeling in my hands and toes and I pondered at what temperature frost bite would occur, maybe I was just being silly.

As we must I soldiered on, or tried too. It couldn’t have been colder than -5 Celsius but having been out all night it felt like the coldest I have ever been. I found shelter under a bridge about 5 km’s down the road and I cooked up some oats and made some coffee while I waited for sunrise.

It was in this moment that I felt truly lost. Cooking oats under a bridge while cars passed above me. It made me feel unworthy in some way. This wasn’t the romantic outdoors, this was, um, homelessness. My tent was so wet it was dripping, my sleeping bag could barely fit it in its bag and my AquaDry jacket was now AquaWet which left me without a protective barrier. “What am I doing?”, I asked myself, “how did I get myself into this position?”. Everything I now owned was packed onto the back of this bicycle I called Zen. I have no home and no idea where I am going or what I am going towards. “What is my future?”

In that moment I could have easily given up. I could have headed to an airport and flown home. It was the sheer realisation that I had no home, that I had nowhere to fly to, it was that fact and that alone that resolved me to continue. I had to see this through and hopefully find myself. Saying that, I would take a small break I deserved that much and my gear needed to dry off anyway. I hoped on my emergency 4G and booked into the cheapest motel I could find which was 70 km’s away.

It turned out to be a long hard day of cycling, probably my hardest so far. I skipped lunch, took few breaks, battled icy roads and dodged swerving cars. All in an attempt to make it to this motel and regroup.

I am now sitting in a nearby Mc Donalds preparing to set off tomorrow. My gear is all dry and reproofed with waterproofing spray, I am warm and feeling optimistic. I feel ready to continue to brave this road further at least for now.

Will I make it the remaining 1400km (as the crow flies) or will this road end up breaking me? I can’t say for certain which way this pursuit will go, but I can only hope that in this, one of my greatest challenges, I find some semblance of meaning which guides me into the future.
