item.title: Day Eight: The Reality of Solo Cycle Touring in the Rain
item.description: Trading companionship for independence, surviving icy roads, and fixing my first flat tire as the solo leg of the trip begins.
item.content:encoded:
The wind was blowing 22km/h from the South which meant I was against it all day. I was wet and so was everything else. Strangely the cycling was turning out to be the easiest part of the journey.

The alarm buzzed early on day 7, I was on the top bunk and as the ladder was blocked by the bed we turned up I had to fling myself over the edge and shut it off. There’s no snooze needed after that activity I tell you!

It took me longer than usual to get ready because of some changes I had made to my packing and there was even a moment I feared it wouldn’t all fit in. When I look at what I have left of my possessions laid out on the floor it looks like very little but trying to fit it all into bags and on the bike makes me think I have too much.

There was a moment of apprehension and we discussed changing plans again and continuing the journey together, but we felt that the wheels were already in motion and we should continue on as planned. Going off on my own scared me so much I felt I had no choice but to do it.

I spent 20 minutes or so fine tuning my brakes and gears after the cable swap the days before and found the bike to be much more responsive, a good thing as the roads were still covered in ice and snow and I needed all the stopping power I could muster. Luckily the storm had passed over us and it was shaping up to be a beautiful day with blue skies and sunshine. The weather really does change quick!

In all honesty there couldn’t have been a better day to make my first few kilometres alone. The views were iconic and the melting snow coupled with the green fields really made me feel at ease.

After a coffee break at a local cafe, lunch on the side of the road, peanut butter on a baguette and lots and lots of cycling, I managed to find a semi dry plot of land to camp.

I was cautious not to disturb the neighbours who seemed to be close by and used my red light torch to construct the tent and cook up some dinner on my newly purchased camp stove.

It gets dark really quick in winter when you have no electricity and I was blessed with an amazing view of the stars, not quite outdoor country but much more than I had seen in a long time. I slept like a baby.

Day 8: I woke up early as I must have gone to bed really early the night before. The pitter patter of the rain drops was soothing yet disturbing at the same time. A meditation session helped and before I knew it, it was time to start packing up.

I was in no rush and took my time with breakfast and a coffee before drying off my tent and packing it up. It seemed peaceful for the most part until I was starting to be surrounded by farmers in their tractors. This gave me the oomph I really needed to get out of there!

It took me about 6km to get back onto the road heading South. Everything really looks different in the daylight. The roads were quiet and it was raining on and off, not heavy but enough to saturate you with water over a period of time. To prevent me from losing hope and falling into dispair the Sun would pop out just often enough to put a smile on my face.

Then all of a sudden the road got really bumpy and I lost control of my steering. I had my first flat tire. It was the front tire which made it easy to remove and fix, thank you quick release! It seemed to rain harder while I was patching the puncture and by the time it was replaced I was ready for a coffee and a place to dry off.

The nearest town gave me shelter at a local pub where I enjoyed a grande cafe and a cheeky bowl of fries. I asked for some tap water to replenish my stock and headed back out to make up my lost kilometres.

After cycling in the rain most of the day I was buzzing with joy when I found an isolated camp spot and pitched a tent. It’s time to dry off, eat up and get warm.

In total I managed 51km today despite the wind. Adding that to the 77km from yesterday puts me at 374km and 1 week on the road. The freedom is amazing, the fear of the unknown is taking some time to get used to.

item.title: Day 6: Snowstorms, Broken Gear, and Going Solo in France
item.description: Sub-zero temperatures, failing stoves, and trail-side arguments test our limits as a two-man cycle tour starts to unravel in the snow.
item.content:encoded:
Snow made a scraping noise as it slid off the side of my tent. The alarm was buzzing alerting us its time to pack up camp to avoid detection. I sat up and watched the steam come off my breathe thinking ‘Wow, this is intense!’

We haven’t covered much ground over the last 4 days, some essential repairs on Dave set us back and caused us to stay in Calais an extra night than intended. It wasn’t bad though we were in a motel. We had hot water, heating and wifi. Things could have easily been worse.

The majority of day 3 was spent replacing some parts of Dave’s drive train which turned out to have more problems than originally expected. We were forced to do this in the cold for lack of a better space which slowed us down considerably. The job ended up unfinished as we headed in for a warm meal and drink.

Day 4 was an early start, we planned to cover some ground and make up for lost time. While still cold the sky was blue and it was a beautiful day. The perfect day for cycling. The weather showed snow for the next day so we knew it wouldn’t last. The ride started off good but then we started to see steeper ups and downs which forced us to stop in a forest and do some work on Dave’s brakes. Replacing the pads and fine tuning resolved the issues but it cost us valuable daylight. These things always end up being more finicky than you expect.

The beauty of the forest was magnified by the sun that shone on just the right angle to hit the trees and make them glow. The absolute silence added to the moment encouraging a peaceful mind. It was cold but not too cold, rather the type of cold that makes you appreciate your own warmth. It seemed the perfect place for a meditation session, and indeed it was.

We headed out cycling until dark, heading South and navigating purely by the sun. There was something romantic about using the sun as a navigation aid however this method did cause us to take a less than direct route. We scouted 4 sites before finally finding ground that was equally dry and secluded enough for wild camping. We set up camp taking care not to upset any locals or damage anything. We had only managed 30km for the day, but this wasn’t a race and I had all the time in the world.

A coffee would have been the perfect companion at this point and so I broke out the trusty Roben Firefly stove and started boiling some water. Old Roben Firefly was not so trusty after all and I just barely managed to warm up some water after a good 20 minutes of cook time. I thought it might have just been because the gas was so cold and accepted my warm coffee before climbing into my sleeping bag with a book and a headlamp.

It wasn’t long and we were both out cold, literally cold. It rained most of the night and began snowing early the next morning. My feet were cold all night but luckily the rest of me remained adequately warm. I must have been touching the bottom sides of my tent with my sleeping bag and bringing in the cold into my toes.

Day 5 started off with a bang and I was determined to head out before light so that we would not be seen. I packed my gear leaving my tent standing and attempted to boil some water. This time I had spent the last hour in bed with my gas canister heating it up. The stove lit, burned for a second and immediately died. I could not relight it after this. Something was wrong.

I had already been out the tent twice by this point and I was conscious of all the snow and ice I was bringing back into the tent so after dismantling most of my stove and realising I needed more tools off my bike to finish the job I decided to settle for no coffee and just drank cold water instead.

The weather was bad! There was a strong wind, very little visibility and it was snowing. We opted to wait out the storm before moving on. Inevitably I fell back to sleep and eventually woke up once it was quieter outside. We managed to pack up our gear and clear camp just as it started raining again. The puddles of water left behind were the tents were showed the extent of our problems.

Tensions were up and we had a small argument about continuing the journey together before opting to move on to the nearest town to regroup. This meant heading hard West completely off our intended course. It looked like we were facing a storm and the winds were reported to be up to 77km/h. There were points along our journey that we just couldn’t cycle or even walk but instead just stood on one side of the bikes leaning into the wind bracing as much as possible and taking a couple steps as it subsided before repeating the same again. The wind was strong and it was scary at one point it lifted me and my bike back a few centimeters. Being high up on a hill surrounded by open fields didn’t help the matter. I couldn’t help but giggle at the difficulty involved in moving forward.

We saw that the weather was meant to be getting worse the next day before clearing up for Tuesday and decided to head back indoors and wait it out. We booked the cheapest motel we could find for two nights. Which turned out to be perfect as it had a bunk bed and a single bed off to the side. We raised the single bed up into a corner creating ample work space for bike maintenance.

I spent most of the night working on Zen. I wrapped her bars with new tape for comfort, replaced the gear and brake cables and gave a final tune up. All parts these parts I had been carrying for emergencies but I decided to use them and clear some room for food in my panniers.

The recent events had caused some dissent in the group. The journey was looking much more difficult than we had thought and difficult challenges always bring up emotions. My travel companion decided he wanted some time to think about what he was doing. We agreed to part ways later in the week while he went to a meditation camp to decide what he wanted to do going forward. I would carry on my route and he may join me later if that he felt he wanted to continue on. For now we would wait out the storm together.

I woke up this morning feeling fresh and ready to go, but knowing full well I would be stuck in Saint-Martin-Boulogne for another day and night. With 40km/h winds, snow and sleet this was not a good day for cycling. At least the weather is set to be clear tomorrow. The time stuck indoors gives me the opportunity to dry out my gear, service my bike and of course update you readers. It is much appreciated time.

Now 6 days in and we have travelled 130km from London to Dover, 80km from Dover to Calais by Ferry, 30km South from Calais to Alincthun and then 15km West to Saint-Martin-Boulogne. We have covered a distance of 255km with 175km by bicycle. This puts us at 29km per day on average far below my goal of 66km. It is important to remember that this is not a race and that the lessons come in the journey not at the finish line.

My spirits are high and I’m excited to carry on braving this weather which looks to get better as I head South. Travelling alone does not scare me even though it will change the dynamic of the trip so far. Even in the most trialing of moments there are glimmers of hope to get you through. All you need is love.

item.title: Day 2: Stormy Tent Nights, Ferry Seasickness, and Arriving in France
item.description: Battling howling winds, a broken bike rack, rough seas, and finally touching down in Calais on day two of our cycle tour.
item.content:encoded:
A Stormy Awakening

Sleeping was near impossible! The wind howled like a hungry wolf while the rain punished the polyester cover we called home. Outside I could hear the flapping of a loose tarp; which kept me from getting any deep rest. There was no chance I was going outside in that weather! I’m sure you can relate. Mostimes Sometimes I’d rather just put up with annoyance rather than leave my bed. Patience or laziness? You tell me.

This being the first night I had some trouble trusting things would be ok. The loudest thought in my mind was that our gear and bicycles would be snatched away by a silent thief. And to be honest with the noise going on outside, he wouldn’t even need to be that silent. Maybe trust is something I will learn from this passage.

The Morning Rush

The alarm rang at 6 am. Despite being tired I welcomed the noise. No more pretending trying to sleep! We had one hour to pack up our gear. Another two hours were planned in for our cycle to the port. With our ferry leaving at 10 am that should have been sufficient.

It was warm enough in the tent which made getting dressed easier. Outside was another story. The cold was in my bones and the rain caressed my now wet clothes (waterproofs for the win!). I could sense the annoyance in my companions aura body language.

Aha! You know that tail wagging I told you about yesterday? It was caused by a missing bolt on Zen’s (my mechanical steed) rear rack. And the mystery is solved. I love it when a troubling problem ends with a simple solution. I dug out a replacement and just like that sorted (I’m handy like that).

With the bikes loaded, we set off. I was optimistic, after all, it was the first day. This view was not shared and I did my best to limit our conversation. Only one day in from a comfortable London flat and waking up indoors is replaced by the cold, rain and wind. Who can blame him!

We’re late, late for an important date! The cycle was a hurried mess. The strong wind threw us around the road and google maps got us lost. We just didn’t want to be outside any longer. Our tickets were only £25 but as they were non-refundable we didn’t want to miss boarding. You could call it money practice for the road. #thrifty

Getting thrown in the deep end like this meant we faced some apprehension about continuing onward. Rather than stop, we decided to talk about it at breakfast. On the ferry, in the warmth, over a coffee (cannot wait).

Crossing the Channel

Yeah ok, so we were a little late. But crucially late for boarding and not for departure. After checking with her boss, the women at the desk let us board. I heard him say “they were exposed to the elements” (love you, bro). We followed a painted line which led us where we needed to be.

Bikes on board, balancing carefully in the hold we head upstairs for breakfast. Ha-lle-lu-jah! The vegetarian breakfast became vegan by dropping the eggs and we sat down to eat. I shouldn’t leave out the coffee, it wasn’t great but the warmth was well needed. It soothed our aching bones.

Once satisfied and warm it was time to discuss our future. Personally, I was happy to continue on. After sharing how hard the morning had been, his doubts and fears we both agreed on the same. We did, however, make one alteration, our route. Instead of going coastal we would go inland. We thought the weather might be better.

I had only ever been seasick once in my life, this made it twice. I say seasick but really I mean little queasy. Sleeping sorted me out (like it does for most things). The waters were really rough to be fair. Our neighbours, a school group, weren’t so lucky and the floor quickly changed colour.

Becoming Tourists

We carefully returned to our bikes after docking. Taking great care to avoid any area of the floor that was not the same colour it had been when we boarded.

Slight confusion ensued while we were reminded that the French drive on the other side of the road (whoops!). It was still raining and we didn’t really know what to do next. After visiting the tourist information centre we checked into the cheapest hotel in town, with available beds. The room was plain and simple, and just what we needed. Make it to Calais, check!

Wow, I’m not entirely sure I expected our journey to pan out this way. Perhaps it was not well thought out. Or maybe we are not well enough equipped to handle such a grand undertaking. I can only hope that each passing day gets a little easier. Plus if you face the most difficult situations to start everything after it is a picnic, right?! #WhenInDoubtOptimismsTheShout

At least our deadlines are now over. Well most of them, besides for reaching Lisbon by the 9th January we are free as birds (the non-caged ones)! That is kind of a relief because we have no idea what we are going to do next!

item.title: Day 1: 130 Kilometers, Broken Gear, and Surviving Our First Day on Bikes
item.description: A brutal 130-kilometer awakening, mechanical failures, and navigating out of London on the very first day of our cycle tour to Lisbon.
item.content:encoded:
Early Mornings

A sudden jerk shifted me out of my dream state. My subconsciousness’s attempt to incorporate the melodic beeping into my dream had failed. This signals the start of the beginning. Reality doesn’t manage to set in until you are brushing the sleep from your eyes much earlier than you normally would.

One hundred and thirty kilometres! That is what we are facing today. I think know I haven’t even cycled that far in the last three years combined.

As is often the case it was difficult getting myself prepared in the morning (I love a sleep in). Something in the back of my mind tempted me to climb back into bed and forget about the whole thing. I pushed it back into the depths it belongs. I often find it strange how sleep seems to solve any problem (until you wake up). But there was no turning back now though, the proverbial ship had sailed.

We loaded up the bicycles, hereafter referred to as Zen and Dave. Zen would be my noble steed, after her model name Zenith. And Dave was, well Dave. Breakfast was quick and rushed. My main priority was ensuring I left the house in a good condition. I was counting on receiving the deposit to help fund my journey. The last thing I wanted was a deduction for something I could easily have rectified.

Escaping London

Despite our most optimistic intentions to leave the house by 5:30 am we eventually set off around 7 am. The air was chilly and it felt fresh as it entered my lungs. An odd statement to make in a big city like London, and I suppose this was going to be an odd day.

It took both us some time to get used to the weight of the bikes. It’s not every day you ride around with 30 kilograms of extra weight. We took special care in ensuring that the weight was evenly distributed on the left and the right. This didn’t make adjusting to the balance any easier.

We soon discovered that London is extraordinarily well set up for cyclists. As we headed South East we mostly had use of either a cycle lane or a dedicated path. Our first few glimpses of what lay ahead came in the form of Zen’s chain slipping off multiple times along the way.

Leaving the City Behind

I love boats. It’s something about being on the water that excites me. So I was delighted when we had to catch a ferry across the river at Tilbury. Getting the bikes on the boat while tricky was much easier than I had anticipated.

The further away we got from London to more beautiful the scenery became. We saw more green, fewer cars and it just seemed to be more pleasant. I pondered on the reason I had decided to spend the last three years of my life settled in London. Even more, why had I used it as a base for all of my twenties?!

Now I’m not trying to knock London. It has a hell of a lot to offer. In fact, if there is something you enjoy doing it’s happening in London. Or at the very least on the outskirts of Greater London. Perhaps it was the weather, constant grey skies, or just city life in general. But I never thought of London as home and leaving probably brought me more joy than it should have.

Lunch Time

I had spent yesterday evening marking out points along the way. The reason was for us to have a reference to how we were pacing ourselves. Given that we were attempting a 130-kilometre trek across unknown terrain it seemed like a good idea. Most of you may snark at 130 kilometres but remember I was not prepared for such a cycle. In many ways neither was my bike.

We were making reasonably good time, well for our expected pace. I had estimated we would arrive at our camp spot for 9 pm. Given the duration of the ride, a proper lunch seemed a good idea and we stopped in Rochester for the very same. Gone were the vegan options most London restaurants provided. Instead, we had to improvise by adding and removing ingredients. Unaware at the time this was something I would become very proficient at.

We have 78 kilometres remaining. What was I thinking? At least the bikes were riding strong. When we set off in the morning it seemed very plausible that they would just break apart. I felt I had to be as delicate as possible, this was changing now. They clearly handled the journey better than my legs (shaking uncontrollably) had.

It was the next half of the journey that we really started to feel the pain. We faced hill after hill and as it is the first day we resisted walking any. I say resisted because it was inevitable in the end. This slowed us down and we quickly slipped behind the mock schedule.

Wrong Turns and Old Villages

I have lost faith in the google maps cycle routes. In fairness to them, they do say they are in beta. A few points along the route the expected road turned out to be non-existent. While at others we were clearly riding on highways as cars sped past us just millimetres from the right. We have little other choices at this point but to keep following the route. Corrections will need to be made as appropriate.

The little towns we passed through on the way sparked curiosity. Coming from South Africa (a newer country), I tend to find these older villages enticing. I wonder about the lives of the people who passed before me and how their village has changed since.

Darkness is Upon Us

Everything went from exciting and new to old and tedious as the sun began to set. With less light, I wasn’t able to enjoy as much of the surroundings. The cycle seemed to become more of a race to the finish. We might have bitten off more than we can chew.

We took our last stop in Faversham as we settled into a local chain pub for some dinner. With vegan options, winning! After resting for a moment all the aches and pains I had hoped would not appear, appeared. The worst of which was an ache in the front of my left knee. You really need your knees if you are embarking on a 2000 something kilometre journey. Especially when you’re only on day one!

I’m not sure if it was the exhaustion, the dark or the sheer amount of hills we were climbing. But something made the last fifth of this ride seem harder and longer than all the others combined.

Gear Failure and Duct Tape Fixes

My bike, Zen, started to show difficulty shifting gears before the front derailleur failed completely. I complained about my limited gear ratios only to find out that Dave had the same problem ever since we left my old house. With my eyes on the prize, getting to the campsite, it seemed wise not to tinker right then.

Somehow, almost miraculously I noticed Dave’s rear-right pannier bag had ripped down the bottom seam. It was then that I heard about an early crash that I had missed. What planet was I on to miss a crash with my only partner?!

Slipped chains, flat tires, failed brakes, sure. But the last thing we expected was problems with our German made pannier bags. Each carrying 5-year guarantees. This was a harsh blow! These bags were waterproof and our only protection against the elements. Without that waterproof seal, there could be problems with wet gear.

Fear not! To fix any problem you need one of two things. Duct tape if it moves and shouldn’t. WD40 or Q20 if it doesn’t move and should. In this case, we opted for the duct tape as it was also water resistant. A quick DIY patch was made and we hoped for the best as we headed on into the distance.

Hitting the Wall

The final stretch was a killer! We faced dark, off-road paths which we could not cycle. The cold had become unbearable and we were constantly getting lost. Could this really be day one? My legs were aching like mad. I could no longer shift into my lowest gears. The balance of my bike had seemingly got worse as I began to notice more and more of a tail wag. How could we possibly make another thirty days of this?

Against all odds, we arrived at our campsite just before midnight. We moved fast, unpacking only the essentials as we prepared for bed. The wind was strong. It seemed to laugh at us as we were served our final struggle for the day. Once inside the tent, despite it all, I slept like a baby. 130 kilometres in one day, that is most definitely a record for me. Perhaps if I can survive this the rest won’t be so bad after all!

It’s a bittersweet thing! I’d love to be with you guys, but I’m also set for this adventure. Hopefully, we will see each other soon. And thank you for reading;)

item.title: Scrapping 2018: Why I Left London and Sold Everything I Owned
item.description: A quarter-life crisis, a chat with dad, and the radical decision to downsize a life in London for an uncertain road trip to Lisbon.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-seventeen has been one heck of a year. It blows my mind the number of changes that have come my way. Smoking went out the window in January. February saw me alcohol-free. I finally began my vegan transformation in April. Trying to express all the lessons I have learnt is not even conceivable.

Hitting Rock Bottom at Twenty-Nine

With the big ‘three O’ birthday coming in twenty-eighteen I’ve hit a quarter-life crisis. One day I just woke up and realised that I wasn’t happy. Despite all the hard work I had put in to get where I was. But change is scary so I did what every twenty-something millennial does when facing difficulties. I called dad.

The Decision

Dad has always been very supportive of my creative whims. I think in some ways he tries to live through me. If ever I found myself unsure about something I could count on dad to motivate me into action.

Needless to say, his advice was to scrap twenty eighteen. Live the year on a whim and see where it took me. It’s hard to argue with your parents so I got started doing just that.

The first step proved most difficult. I battled opposing thoughts for days as I tried to decide what I would do. This proved futile and I eventually realised I had no idea what I wanted.

Take two meant I would list all the things I did not want. I would then make plans that did not include anything on that list. This was surprisingly easy. Who would have thought it would be easier to list what you don’t want than what you do.

It came down to two simple actions. I needed to leave London (for good) and I needed to change my career (completely). Everything else would work out if I just made these two small changes. Granted there was a whole lot of faith in that theory.

As Luck Would Have It

It just so happened that a friend of mine was going through a similar crisis. He had just quit his job and was about to commence on a bicycle tour to Lisbon. We met for coffee and by the time I left we had made arrangements for me to drive us to Lisbon.

For a long time, I had romantic imaginings of a European road trip and this excited me. The steps that followed moved surprisingly quick. Quit job, check. Serve notice on flat, check. Notify those who need to know, check. Sell almost everything I own, check.

Impressively within one month, the remains of my possessions could fit into my 2006 Peugeot 206 and my bank balance was much heavier. I started to mentally prepare myself for life on the road. I slept on the floor. The heating stayed off and the window stayed open. My cooking was done out of one pot and I drank from the same cup.

My notice finished before my friends. This gave me time to prepare, plan, and imagine. I took regular walks in the local forest and started practising my knots. Rubbing sticks to make fire was a challenge I have still to master. Thankfully I carry a jet flame!

In hindsight, the biggest difficulty I faced was letting go of the things I had come to hold dear. I wanted to keep some things that just wouldn’t serve me on the road. My Egyptian cotton sheets almost brought tears to my eyes when they left. While parting with my guitar was a bittersweet experience.

Trading Luxury for Freedom

The last big item I owned was the car. All of a sudden it seemed like dead weight and I wanted it gone. My recent analysis of the fuel costs might have played a part in that decision.

If I was going to do this trip, I was going to do it right! I sold the car and bought a second-hand bicycle in its place. Second-hand felt more legitimate. I figured parts would be more widely available. And let’s face it we just used to make things better and more reliable in the past.

Embracing Minimalism

With most of my possessions gone, I feel great. Literally like I have less baggage. It is the little step before, the letting go. That really challenges you! I am now a minimalist and it feels incredible.

This is it as if I was never in London I will vanish without a trace. I am happy to have company on this trip. This adventure will bring me closer to my purpose in life, it has to.

The Road to Lisbon

And so begins my pursuit. The current destination is Lisbon and the route is unclear. It is not where I am heading but the road to get there. That is where I expect to find the answers I am looking for.

item.title: Subject X, a Short Story
item.description: A story I started once, and never finished.
item.content:encoded:
Trying to find our place in this world is anything but easy. So many options, so many choices. I feel that sometimes it’s impossible to succeed. Should I follow my heart or the opinion of others. As if tied into something I don’t quite understand. I can see the ropes I’m expected to climb, but I’m not sure where they will take me, or which one I should choose.

I was told once that life has a plan for us, that we have a destiny. I should simply give into the greater goodness. Not concentrate, without planning. Just follow the signs. That if I gave into everything that was around me I would always be in that place where I was supposed to be. I have heard many stories about positive thinking or even watched movies with the likes of ‘The Secret’ and reviewed their philosophies. Even perhaps experimented. By visualizing I have often met success. I have accomplished that which I believed impossible. I have achieved that which I believed un-achievable.

Perhaps it was the mere fact that I never finished what I started, I never managed to succeed that brought me to where I am now. To this frame of mind, this way of thinking. As if a dream had overcome me, I merely followed what was there for me to see, for me to find. The great adventure of a lifetime, the most exciting treasure hunt. The search for self discovery, the search for ideals, for belief, for recognition, for understanding, for truth, and for a future.

The grass was long, thick to the touch, it almost felt hard and dry, yet I could see the life inside it, the vibrant green that it held. As I walked over it I could feel the earth and a shiver ran up my spine. The sky was the most amazing blue, I never knew that such a colour existed and for a moment I contemplated its existence. I would often spend days concocting brainteasers or questioning reality and one of my favourite thoughts was about colour. I would ask myself was my red the same colour that everyone else saw, and if our perception of colour was different what effect did that have on humanity? After all colour is used to describe moods, emotional states, good and evil. One colour can say a thousand things, yet we have no way to share the colour that we see. We have just been taught to call it by a name.

This was one of the hottest days we had in a long time. The air was just the right humidity that the heat was pleasant, and I had a great contentment just being outside, just sharing in this day. My skin was pale, I don’t remember turning this white, I looked lifeless, sickly. I felt tired. I had not been outside for a long time. A very long time. I felt as if my chains had been broken, as I closed my eyes for a second there was a burst of wind, it was refreshing and it shifted my hair out of my face, for that moment I was flying. On the wings of angels I soared the skies. Upon opening my eyes I felt that shiver again rising up my spine, concentrating on the top of my head, forcing a smile onto my face.

The sun reflected onto the shed window in such a way that it turned it into a mirror, I could see my face and as I walked up to it I could see my long black hair, it was dirty and accentuated the black lines under my eyes. I was so pale. I remember when the green in my eyes showed everyone that I was alive, I would change the world. I could not see that light anymore, the green was now dull. How did I let this happen to me, how long had I been lost. With a thousand thoughts running through my mind I felt overwhelmed. I had to take this one step at a time. I had to piece this together bit by bit. This was going to take me awhile. I should eat.

item.title: A Map for the Lost
item.content:encoded:
When you find yourself lost in a difficult situation this may help. I was given some advice by a friend I once knew in Spain.

“When you find yourself in the ditch of the road, stop, close your eyes and look at your star. Decide what you want most in life and go for it with your head and your heart together. Come On!”

I think in this day and age many of us find ourselves lost and confused, with all we have gained we seem to have lost something. An understanding, a connection, some feeling that we are missing something persists. With all our choice it is easy to fill this void temporarily, with alcohol, drugs, artificial connection.

I read an interesting study the other day regarding addiction. By creating a mouse utopia and offering the mice a choice of regular water and cocaine spiked water, the aim was to test the relationship between addiction and connection. What they found was that mice in a happy environment used the drug in very small doses, and some not at all. In comparison isolated mice abused the drug until it induced death. Their findings made them insist that the opposite of addiction was not sobriety, but instead human connection, relationships.

Perhaps we have isolated ourselves from each other. We have been taught to fit in and do what is expected by others. There is a way to read, a way to write, a way to play the guitar, and even a way to pick up girls. We follow the advice of others who have been before us, but even more than that, we believe that it is the only way to progress. Constantly failing to remember that at some point even what is now considered standard was created, invented, established. In all likelihood there exists a better way to do everything we now conceive of.

Decide for yourself, what is the purpose of life. Is it financial success? Superiority in one form or the other? Or perhaps it is simply to live. So I say to you my friends; if you find yourselves lost, look at your star, decide what you want most, and go for it. With your head and your heart together!

item.title: Training Gods
item.description: Reflections on the thought that we are all one, a God in training.
item.content:encoded: If every being on this planet is a reincarnation of me. My only goal is to remind all beings I encounter to love. This should be done by example and not forcefully. All judgments should be forgotten, all resentments forgiven. Because there will be a time when I will meet the current version of me, and I have the choice now to make that a pleasant experience that will guide me in the right direction.
